(CNN) -- Nearly eight years later, Connie Chung still remembers being surprised. "Stonewalling is what gets politicians in trouble, when they ... try to cover up," Connie Chung says. It was one of those television moments that linger in the national consciousness, like Barbara Walters sitting down with Monica Lewinsky, Dan Rather with Saddam Hussein, or Jay Leno asking Hugh Grant what the hell he had been thinking. Chung was with ABC then, and she got the "get" -- the first interview with Gary Condit, the California congressman at the center of the Chandra Levy media frenzy. The former Washington intern, you'll recall, had been found murdered in Rock Creek Park, and law enforcement sources let it be known that the married Condit had been having an affair with her. In an interview airing Sunday on "Reliable Sources" (10 a.m. ET, during CNN's "State of the Union with John King"), Chung says she was surprised when Condit refused to acknowledge the romantic relationship. "Stonewalling is what gets politicians in trouble, when they stonewall or they try to cover up," she says. "I think that the general public and the news media wanted him to be honest, and if he could be honest about that part of the story, then he could be -- then he would be believed when he was answering other questions as to whether or not he had anything to do with her disappearance." I often focus on media excess and media mistakes on the program, but we also try to highlight good journalism. The segment includes two Washington Post reporters, Sari Horwitz and Scott Higham, who cracked the Levy mystery in a 13-part series last year. They did what the D.C. police could not: They identified Ingmar Guandique, an illegal Salvadoran immigrant, as Levy's likely killer. Authorities issued an arrest warrant for the imprisoned suspect this week. But Horwitz and Higham talk about how they were roundly criticized for resurrecting the case and accused of sensationalizing it. It's clear that Levy's case became a huge deal in 2001 because of the Condit connection. At the same time, Chung says, "The news media had changed. This was the gradual evolution of what the news media was doing. There was flavor of the week, the story du jour." The Levy frenzy became the precursor for the missing-women TV melodramas that followed: Laci Peterson, Stacy Peterson, Natalee Holloway. The stories of women who were not celebrities, whom no one had heard of before, became national soap operas because they drove cable and morning show ratings. At least, in Levy's case, the soap opera appears to be drawing to a close.

# Connie Chung’s Gary Condit interview helped write the script for cable news’ ‘missing women’ era

**Analysis**

In August 2001, millions of viewers tuned in to watch Connie Chung question California congressman Gary Condit about Chandra Levy, the 24-year-old federal intern whose disappearance had become a national obsession.

The interview, broadcast on ABC’s “Primetime Thursday,” was billed as Condit’s opportunity to address suspicions surrounding his relationship with Levy. Instead, his guarded answers — especially his refusal to discuss whether the two had been romantically involved — intensified the spectacle.

“I’m not going to respond to those questions,” Condit repeatedly told Chung, while insisting he had nothing to do with Levy’s disappearance.

The exchange now feels like more than an artifact of a lurid Washington scandal. It was an early template for a form of television coverage that would dominate cable news in the years ahead: the intensive, highly personalized treatment of a missing young woman’s case, built around dramatic interviews, speculative panels and a central male figure cast as a possible villain long before the facts were settled.

Levy’s case arrived at a transitional moment. The 24-hour news cycle was already established, but the conventions of the modern missing-person frenzy were still being refined. Her disappearance supplied nearly every element television needed: a young and photogenic victim, a secret relationship with a powerful married man, grieving parents, unanswered questions and the backdrop of Washington.

Chung’s interview turned those ingredients into an event.

## An interview framed like a confrontation

Condit entered the broadcast facing enormous pressure to explain himself. Reports had linked him romantically to Levy, who had disappeared from Washington in May 2001. Condit, then a Democratic representative from California, denied any role in her disappearance but resisted discussing intimate details of their relationship.

That distinction mattered legally. It mattered much less on television.

The interview’s force came from the gap between the question viewers wanted answered and Condit’s determination not to answer it. Chung pressed him on whether he had been “in love” with Levy and whether they had engaged in an affair. Condit returned to a narrower point: He had not harmed her and had cooperated with investigators.

The result was a classic television dynamic. His caution read as evasiveness. His privacy claims sounded, to many viewers, like concealment. Every refusal generated another headline.

The interview did not establish that Condit was connected to Levy’s disappearance. But it helped cement him as the story’s central character. The case was increasingly narrated not simply as a search for a missing woman, but as a Washington morality play about sex, power and suspicion.

Condit was never charged in connection with Levy’s disappearance, and authorities eventually said he was not a suspect. His political career nevertheless collapsed; he lost his congressional primary the following year.

## The victim becomes a character

Levy’s disappearance also demonstrated how television transforms a missing person into a familiar public figure.

Her photographs appeared constantly. Viewers learned about her internship, her ambitions, her family and her private life. Her parents became recurring voices in the coverage. The repetition created emotional intimacy: Audiences who had never met Levy were encouraged to feel they knew her.

That intimacy can be valuable. National attention may generate tips, pressure authorities and keep a case from being forgotten. But it can also flatten a person into a set of television-friendly traits: young, attractive, promising, vulnerable.

Levy’s story fit a pattern later described by critics as “missing white woman syndrome” — the disproportionate attention given to missing young, white and often middle-class women compared with missing people of color, Indigenous women, men, poorer victims and others whose disappearances rarely receive sustained national coverage.

Levy was not simply selected because of race or appearance. Her connection to a member of Congress made the case inherently newsworthy. But the scale and emotional intensity of the coverage revealed which kinds of victims television executives believed could sustain a national audience.

## A preview of what came next

The structure would soon become familiar.

When Laci Peterson disappeared in California in 2002, cable networks devoted enormous attention to her husband, Scott Peterson, his affair and his shifting public image. Unlike Condit, Peterson was later convicted of murdering his wife and their unborn son. Yet the narrative machinery — photographs, family interviews, legal analysts and minute-by-minute scrutiny of a suspicious man — had already been tested during the Levy coverage.

The disappearance of Natalee Holloway in Aruba in 2005 pushed the model further. With little new evidence on many days, television filled hours with interviews, reenactments, speculation and arguments over potential suspects. The case became serialized programming.

Years later, the 2021 disappearance and killing of Gabby Petito showed that the format had not vanished; it had merged with social media. TikTok users, YouTube creators and online sleuths joined cable commentators in analyzing body-camera footage, travel posts and the behavior of Petito’s fiancé, Brian Laundrie. The platform had changed, but the underlying appeal remained: a compelling victim, an intimate relationship under suspicion and a mystery audiences could attempt to solve in real time.

Levy’s case helped demonstrate that missing-person coverage could function simultaneously as journalism, public service and episodic entertainment.

## When suspicion outruns evidence

The danger in that model is that narrative momentum can move faster than verified facts.

Levy’s remains were found in Washington’s Rock Creek Park in 2002, more than a year after she disappeared. Her death was ruled a homicide. Another man, Ingmar Guandique, was convicted in 2010, but that conviction was later vacated amid concerns about prosecution evidence and a key witness. Prosecutors dropped the charges in 2016, saying they could not prove the case beyond a reasonable doubt. Guandique was later deported.

Levy’s killing remains officially unresolved.

That complicated history underscores how incomplete the televised story had been. Condit’s secrecy about an alleged affair was politically and personally consequential, but it was not evidence that he killed Levy. Television’s focus on his demeanor and refusal to answer intimate questions encouraged audiences to treat evasiveness as a proxy for guilt.

The problem was not that Chung questioned him aggressively. Condit was a public official entangled in a major story, and his relationship with Levy was plainly relevant. The problem was the larger media environment, which rewarded repetition and insinuation while the evidence remained scarce.

Once a case is organized around a suspect-shaped figure, alternative possibilities become harder to see. Ambiguity is less satisfying than confrontation. “We do not know” is accurate, but it is rarely compelling television.

## A moment before the news changed

The timing of Chung’s interview adds another layer to its legacy. It aired only weeks before the September 11 terrorist attacks transformed American news priorities. The Levy story, which had dominated the summer, was abruptly displaced by war, terrorism and national security.

But the format survived.

When the immediate post-9/11 period receded, cable news returned to cases that offered emotional stakes, recognizable characters and the possibility of constant updates. Missing women became a dependable genre, particularly during periods when networks lacked a single overriding national story.

Seen today, the Chung-Condit interview looks like a hinge between eras: old-fashioned network star power meeting the emerging demands of nonstop, personality-driven news.

It remains gripping television because Chung understood the central contradiction. Condit wanted viewers to accept his denial while allowing him to withhold the personal information they believed would help them judge it. She kept pressing that contradiction.

But the interview’s deeper significance lies in what surrounded it — the transformation of a tragedy into a national serial, the elevation of one man’s behavior over broader questions and the unequal distribution of media empathy.

Chandra Levy deserved attention. So did thousands of other missing people whose names never became breaking-news banners.

The lesson of the coverage is not that the media cared too much about Levy. It is that television learned to package a particular kind of victim and mystery as an irresistible national drama — and then spent the next two decades repeating the formula.

- The lessons the Levy case still holds for journalists today  

Don’t miss this candid look at the reporting behind the headlines—and the responsibilities news organizations carry when a criminal investigation becomes a national media phenomenon.

counterfactuals.output:
Connie Chung’s 2001 interview with Gary Condit now looks like a hinge point in cable news history: the moment a missing-person case was fully recast as serialized national drama. Condit, then a congressman, acknowledged an affair with intern Chandra Levy but denied involvement in her disappearance. His guarded, lawyerly answers produced little new evidence, yet the interview became an event because television had already assigned him a role—the evasive man at the center of the mystery.

That template would become familiar. Laci Peterson’s murder generated a daily narrative of suspicion, betrayal and courtroom revelation. Stacy Peterson’s disappearance was folded into an even more complicated story about her husband, Drew Peterson, who was later convicted of murdering his previous wife, Kathleen Savio, but has not been charged in Stacy’s disappearance. Natalee Holloway’s disappearance in Aruba became an open-ended summer saga sustained by repeated interviews, speculative leads and the magnetism of an unresolved mystery.

The common denominator was not merely public concern. It was television’s ability to turn uncertainty into programming: recurring characters, ominous music, exclusive sit-downs, incremental “developments” and endless panels discussing what a suspect’s demeanor might mean. Chung’s Condit interview showed both the power and the weakness of that form. A high-profile confrontation can clarify the public record, but it can also create the illusion that performance is evidence.

The Levy case itself ultimately resisted television’s tidy storytelling. Her remains were found in 2002. Ingmar Guandique was convicted of her murder, but that conviction was later vacated and prosecutors dismissed the charges. The case remains officially unsolved. That complicated ending is a reminder that the national soap opera often reaches emotional verdicts long before the justice system reaches—or fails to reach—a factual one.

## Connie Chung recalls Gary Condit’s silence in Chandra Levy case — and the reporting that revived it

Veteran television journalist Connie Chung has recalled her surprise at former congressman Gary Condit’s refusal to answer key questions about missing federal intern Chandra Levy during a nationally televised 2001 interview, an exchange that became one of the most memorable moments in a case that transfixed Washington.

Levy, 24, disappeared in May 2001. Investigators later learned she had been involved with Condit, a married Democratic representative from California. Condit denied any role in her disappearance and was never charged, but his guarded public responses fueled intense scrutiny.

Chung, who interviewed Condit for ABC’s “PrimeTime Thursday” that August, has said she expected him to use the appearance to address the central question surrounding their relationship. Instead, Condit repeatedly declined to discuss whether he had an affair with Levy, saying he would not answer questions about his private life.

The resistance startled Chung because Condit had agreed to a high-profile interview amid escalating speculation. Rather than quieting the controversy, his answers came across as evasive and deepened public suspicion, even though police did not consider him a suspect in Levy’s death.

Levy’s remains were discovered in Washington’s Rock Creek Park in May 2002, a year after she vanished. Her death was ruled a homicide, but the investigation stalled.

Years later, a Washington Post investigation by reporters Sari Horwitz and Scott Higham revisited the case, examining police missteps and focusing renewed attention on Ingmar Guandique, a Salvadoran immigrant who had attacked other women in Rock Creek Park around the time Levy disappeared. The newspaper’s reporting helped revive the dormant investigation and brought Guandique to wider attention as a possible suspect.

Authorities ultimately charged Guandique with Levy’s murder. He was convicted in 2010, largely on circumstantial evidence and testimony from a jailhouse informant. But the conviction was later vacated after serious questions emerged about the informant’s credibility. Prosecutors dropped the charges in 2016, saying they could no longer prove the case beyond a reasonable doubt. Guandique was subsequently deported.

The reversal left Levy’s killing officially unresolved. It also underscored the complex legacy of a case initially dominated by Condit’s political scandal, only to be redirected years later by investigative reporting toward another man — a suspect whose conviction ultimately did not stand.
